questions.question: When is $a_1x_1+\cdots+a_nx_n=d$ a linear subspace rather than merely an affine hyperplane?
questions.explanation: $a_1x_1+\cdots+a_nx_n=d$ is a linear subspace exactly when $d=0$ (so it passes through the origin).
questions.source_support: Hyperplane as subspace or affine set.
questions.review_notes: Manually designed in LA high-quality batch 13; concept-specific stem and plausible distractors.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
questions.skill_detail: conceptual: Hyperplane as subspace or affine set.
option_explanations: $d=1$ gives an affine hyperplane, not a subspace.

The signs of the $a_i$ fix only the orientation of the normal vector $(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$, not whether the set is a subspace; a subspace must contain $\boldsymbol 0$, and substituting gives $a_1\cdot0+\cdots+a_n\cdot0=d$, forcing $d=0$.

The ambient dimension is irrelevant: the origin test $a_1\cdot0+\cdots+a_n\cdot0=d$ forces $d=0$ in every $\mathbb R^n$, so origin-passing hyperplanes are subspaces for $n=2,3,\ldots$ alike, not only for $n=3$.
